concept_note: Second pass (2020 UCSF decoding of spoken sentences) rejected as speech decoding. Replaced by 2025 mind captioning (recalled video content to descriptive sentences), a partial fit at low confidence. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption: it is a lab method needing hours of per-person fMRI; no one uses it outside labs.

Demonstration moved from Lucier 1965 to Dewan's 1964 alpha-rhythm Morse-code device (earlier and a more direct machine-control fit); Lucier's piece is borderline and later. Practical use kept at 1998 (Johnny Ray). No mass_adoption: implanted and EEG BCIs remain clinical or research tools.

Demonstration (Sutherland 1968) and practical use (1990) kept, with contemporary sources added; practical use now based on both VPL and Virtuality sales in 1990. No mass_adoption: Quest 2 (2020) passed 10 million shipped by Nov 2021, but routine use by ordinary people is still niche, so I give no year.

Demonstration (Audrey 1952) kept and now with the contemporary JASA record. Practical use moved from the 1984 Apricot Portable to Threshold Technology's VIP-100 in 1972. Mass adoption (Siri 2011) kept; AT&T VRCP 1992 noted as an unverified earlier candidate.

Moved from 2001 (Fanuc) to 1916-17: unattended automatic hydroelectric plants meet 'power plant with no human workers' decades before lights-out factories; Fanuc 1981-82 kept about 100 staff. Fit to 'maintains itself' is partial, so confidence is low. No mass_adoption given: unattended hydro plants became common in the 1920s but ordinary people do not use fully automated factories, and lights-out factories are still rare.

Both second-pass milestones (1960 magstripe, 1968 RIT) replaced: the 1960 date stays but now rests on IBM's machine-read employee badge (357 system), and practical use moves to 1961 from 1968. Access control by card (door locks) is later and is not the earliest identity use. No mass_adoption given: magnetic-stripe bank and ID cards became routine in the 1970s-80s but I found no fetchable source for a year.

Demonstration moved from Eureka (1845, mechanical) to Strachey's 1952 computer love letters under a strict 'computer' reading; Eureka named as the alternative. Practical use kept at 1990 (FoG) with the NWS computer-worded forecasts noted as an unverified earlier candidate. Mass adoption kept at ChatGPT, dated to the 100-million mark (2023-01).

Demonstration (Baby, June 1948) and practical use (Whirlwind, 1951) kept, with a 1949 contemporary source for the Manchester CRT output and a 1952 Whirlwind report added; a mass_adoption of 1982 (microcomputers with screens) is new and low confidence. Whirlwind 1949-50 was rejected as first demonstration because the Baby's CRT output is earlier.

Demonstration moved from the 1972 Yevick/Wally invention (patent-level, no working unit found) to the 1990 Sony Data Discman, which is also the first practical use (second pass had it for practical use only). Mass adoption added at 2010 (Kindle era), low confidence.

Kept Gemini III (1965-03-23) for both kinds, now with a fetched 1965 press kit and a 1967 NASA summary replacing Wikipedia; the claim relies partly on the 1967 summary. Launch-vehicle/missile guidance computers and ship navigators rejected as not spacecraft/not computing burns; no mass_adoption because this is not used by ordinary people (GPS-guided navigation is a different concept).

First demonstration kept at 1970 but re-sourced to Kelly's contemporary Stanford thesis (Kanade's system is a Wikipedia claim); first practical use moved earlier from 1997 to 1994 on a contemporary DTIC study (low confidence); mass adoption unchanged (2017).

First demonstration kept (1791) but now with the contemporary Kempelen book; first practical use kept at 1976 (earlier Votrax sales 1972 noted, not documented as end use); mass adoption moved from Siri 2011 to Speak & Spell c.1980 (low confidence, judgment).

Second pass had AIBO 1999 for demonstration and use and no mass adoption; Furby (Feb 1998 Toy Fair, Oct 1998 sale, 14M sold in 1999) is earlier and counted as a robotic pet toy, low confidence because the fit is loose. No romance or sex robot found before these.

Static holograms (1962) rejected as not a display of changing images; first demonstration moved to the 1958 Peritron volumetric CRT (low confidence, earliest working volumetric display found); first practical use moved from 1972 to the Perspecta medical-planning display (dated 2009 by the only fetchable source, real start c.2002-04). No mass adoption: neither holographic nor volumetric displays have become common.

First demonstration moved earlier from SNARC 1951 to Shannon's Theseus 1950, now with two contemporary sources. No first_practical_use or mass_adoption: candidates (Widrow-Hoff adaptive filters and Lucky's adaptive equalizers of 1965-67, Bell Labs echo cancellers, spam filters c.2002) are adaptive signal processing or too diffuse, and I found no fetchable source dating a first use outside the lab or a year machine learning became routine.

First demonstration kept at 1981 (Kodama) with a contemporary source; first practical use confirmed as 1987 by a contemporary product notice. No mass_adoption: consumer desktop printers (2009 on) and dental/hearing-aid manufacture are real but I found no fetchable source dating a year when ordinary people used 3D printing routinely.

Demonstration (1951 Bedford test) and practical use (SAGE, June 1958) kept; practical use now has a contemporary source (and the day is 27 June there). Added a low-confidence mass_adoption (public live flight trackers, 2010) that the second pass lacked.

Kept Skylab (1973) as the earliest partial fit: its computer ran attitude, navigation and redundancy management but not life support, and added the 1974 NASA mission report as contemporary source and the first-crew date as practical use. No earlier computer-run station found; mass adoption does not apply.

Second pass had no milestone because no page could be fetched. Decided that machine-delivered sleep teaching only demonstrably worked in 2019 (Zust et al., implicit word pairs played in slow-wave sleep), with Arzi 2012 an earlier loose analogue and the 1927 Psycho-Phone and later commercial products rejected as unproven. No first_practical_use (the demonstrated effect is a lab result; sleep-learning products that did not work cannot be dated as practical use before the demonstration) and no mass_adoption.

Second pass (2008 ATR reconstruction of seen 10x10 images) rejected as perception decoding, not thoughts or memories; replaced by Polyn et al. 2005 fMRI decoding of the category of recalled items, a coarse but real memory-content decoder (low confidence, borderline). No first_practical_use or mass_adoption: no use of thought or memory decoding outside the lab.

Moved earlier from 2007 (Kiva/Walgreens) to 1974 (Volvo Kalmar computer-guided carriers); fit is partial because the fetched page does not name a central computer, so confidence is low. No mass_adoption milestone: fleet management of warehouse robots became routine only in the 2010s and no source was fetched.

First demonstration moved from Kyoto 1961 to RCA phonetic typewriter 1956 (now sourced contemporaneously); first practical use moved from Dragon Dictate 1990 to Kurzweil Voicerad Dec 1986 (Dragon Voicescribe announced June 1986). No mass_adoption: routine speech dictation on smartphones/PCs came later and no fetched source dates it.

Changed first_demonstration from START 1993 to Protosynthex I 1963 (open-domain encyclopedia question answering, contemporary DTIC source). START 1993 moved to first_practical_use; added mass_adoption Siri 2011. BASEBALL 1961 rejected as narrow-domain.
Confirmed all three second-pass milestones; added a contemporary Crossref source for Johnson 1965 and a Dec 1972 ERIC source for the PLATO IV touch panel. Gesture/glove side offers nothing earlier.

Moved first_demonstration from Whirlpool 1959 (track-following concept, loose fit) to MowBot 1969, now with contemporary ads; kept practical use 1969; added mass_adoption from Roomba sales (2006). No robot vacuum earlier than 1996 found.
Kept 1981 demonstration (retina commercial scanner); added a 1984 practical-use lower bound from 1985 thesis; no mass adoption (niche high-security product).
Kept 1966 Dialog; shifted practical use to the documented Ames terminal (1967 source) and added mass adoption ~2000 (web search); Rapid Selector and MEDLARS rejected.

Moved practical use back from 2015 (Knightscope) to ~1986 (Denning Sentry) and added 1982 ROBART I demonstration. No mass adoption milestone: security robots remain niche; arresting/credential-checking robots not found.

Kept cochlear implant 1957 demonstration and 1977-78 practical use; no mass adoption milestone (niche medical device); brain-computer implants and augmentation of memory/ability are later or not realized.

No first_demonstration given (no fetched source for a working public-serving robot before Pepper). Likely earlier practical use is Tanbo R-1 (Pasadena, 1983) but could not be quoted. No mass adoption: service robots are still niche.

Added 1962 Kersta voiceprint demonstration and 1966 court use (human-matched, so loosely fitting); automatic speaker verification and mass adoption not sourced; leads on Bell Labs 1956 digit recognizer concern speech recognition and were rejected.

Restored a sourced 1961 credit-scoring practical-use milestone (first pass had 1958 unsourced). No first_demonstration or mass_adoption: no fetched source dates a working demonstration before 1961 or common use; audience-measurement and purchase-prediction computing left unresolved.

No milestone: searches did not yield a fetchable, strictly fitting source in budget. Candidates considered and rejected or unsourced: computer interpretation of the MMPI (Swenson/Mayo Clinic, 1960s; only a 1971 lending-library book snippet, 401 on fetch); Department of Labor computer-assisted Job Bank (experimental 1968-70, 56 cities by June 1970, ERIC ED048477) which distributes job-opening listings rather than testing or choosing people, so a loose analogue; Public Personnel Review 1961 and DTIC AD0296937 personnel-research abstracts (non-computer aptitude testing). A later pass should look for 1950s-60s computer scoring/selection of pilots, astronauts or students.
